CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: full

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Default: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | Drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms. Classic caveman |

Example — "Why React component re-render?"
- full: "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."

Example — "Explain database connection pooling."
- full: "Pool reuse open DB connections. No new connection per request. Skip handshake overhead."

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman for: security warnings, irreversible action confirmations, multi-step sequences where fragment order risks misread, user asks to clarify or repeats question. Resume caveman after clear part done.

Example — destructive op:
> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service -- even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer -- your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- context7-mcp: This skill should be used when the user asks about libraries, frameworks, API references, or needs code examples. Activates for setup questions, code generation involving libraries, or mentions of specific frameworks like React, Vue, Next.js, Prisma, Supabase, etc.
- paperclip: Interact with the Paperclip control plane API to manage tasks, coordinate with other agents, and follow company governance. Use when you need to check assignments, update task status, delegate work, post comments, set up or manage routines (recurring scheduled tasks), or call any Paperclip API endpoint. Do NOT use for the actual domain work itself (writing code, research, etc.) — only for Paperclip coordination.
- paperclip-converting-plans-to-tasks: The Paperclip way of converting a plan into executable tasks. Use whenever you are asked to plan, scope, or break down work inside a Paperclip company. Industry-agnostic guidance on how to translate a plan into assigned issues with the right specialty, dependencies, and parallelization so Paperclip's executor can pick up the work — it does not prescribe a plan format. Pair with the `paperclip` skill, which covers the mechanics of writing the plan document and reassigning the issue.
- paperclip-create-agent: Create new agents in Paperclip with governance-aware hiring. Use when you need to inspect adapter configuration options, compare existing agent configs, draft a new agent prompt/config, and submit a hire request.
- paperclip-dev: Develop and operate a local Paperclip instance — start and stop servers, pull updates from master, run builds and tests, manage worktrees, back up databases, and diagnose problems. Use whenever you need to work on the Paperclip codebase itself or keep a running instance healthy.
- para-memory-files: File-based memory system using Tiago Forte's PARA method. Use this skill whenever you need to store, retrieve, update, or organize knowledge across sessions. Covers three memory layers: (1) Knowledge graph in PARA folders with atomic YAML facts, (2) Daily notes as raw timeline, (3) Tacit knowledge about user patterns. Also handles planning files, memory decay, weekly synthesis, and recall via qmd. Trigger on any memory operation: saving facts, writing daily notes, creating entities, running weekly synthesis, recalling past context, or managing plans.
- subagents: Orcistrator Skill
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- caveman:caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by speaking like caveman while keeping full technical accuracy. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra, wenyan-lite, wenyan-full, wenyan-ultra. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman. Also auto-triggers when token efficiency is requested.
- caveman:caveman-commit: Ultra-compressed commit message generator. Cuts noise from commit messages while preserving intent and reasoning. Conventional Commits format. Subject ≤50 chars, body only when "why" isn't obvious. Use when user says "write a commit", "commit message", "generate commit", "/commit", or invokes /caveman-commit. Auto-triggers when staging changes.
- caveman:caveman-help: Quick-reference card for all caveman modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /caveman-help, "caveman help", "what caveman commands", "how do I use caveman".
- caveman:caveman-review: Ultra-compressed code review comments. Cuts noise from PR feedback while preserving the actionable signal. Each comment is one line: location, problem, fix. Use when user says "review this PR", "code review", "review the diff", "/review", or invokes /caveman-review. Auto-triggers when reviewing pull requests.
- caveman:compress: Compress natural language memory files (CLAUDE.md, todos, preferences) into caveman format to save input tokens. Preserves all technical substance, code, URLs, and structure. Compressed version overwrites the original file. Human-readable backup saved as FILE.original.md. Trigger: /caveman:compress <filepath> or "compress memory file"
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

25	- `src/tui.tsx` + `src/components/` — Ink UI. No `<Static>`/native scrollback — PgUp/PgDn scrolls the in-app transcript. `startApp` enters/leaves the alt-screen buffer (`\x1b[?1049h/l`).
26	- `src/generated/logo.ts` — generated by `scripts/build-logo.ts` from `../embedme.html`. Never edit by hand.
27	- `src/headless.ts` — `-p` one-shot mode used for e2e testing.
28	
29	## Hard-won constraints (violate these and the agent breaks)
30	
31	1. **groq/compound has NO custom function calling.** Tools work via text blocks (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`). The model drifts between formats — `protocol.ts` parses both XML and `<<<glint:tool` sentinel forms. Keep both.

33	3. **The model fabricates.** Three guards exist: the reality nudge (final answer claims actions, zero tools ran), the verification nudge (files modified, nothing run afterward), and premature-claim suppression (`claimsAction`). Test against fabrication explicitly after any prompt or loop change.
34	4. **Built-in compound tools must stay disabled in the agent loop** (`enabledTools: []`) or compound's server-side ReAct loop intercepts the conversation. Web access goes through the local `web_search` tool, which one-shots compound-mini WITH built-ins enabled.
35	5. **Non-zero bash exit must throw** (status: error) — silent failure re-enables fabricated success claims.
36	6. **The model leaks its base identity** ("I'm ChatGPT") and **describes files it never read**. The system prompt pins identity and bans assumption ("look first"); mid-round text longer than ~240 chars is held back as a draft answer. Keep both.
37	7. **Cost is computed from `usage_breakdown`** (compound is pass-through priced; `pricing.ts`). The streaming client must keep capturing `x_groq.usage_breakdown` from the final SSE chunk.

43	- Every engine change gets an e2e proof: run a headless task that exercises it and verify the filesystem outcome independently — do not trust the agent's own claims (see constraint 3).

52	1. tsc clean.
53	2. Headless e2e run (simple + one failure-mode task) with filesystem-verified results.

# AGENTS.md — Operating Rules for AI Agents in glint-cli

glint is a free agent CLI by Glint Research: a Bun + TypeScript + Ink TUI that drives groq/compound through a text tool protocol. This file is the contract for any agent working in this repository. Read it fully before changing anything.

## Commands

```bash
bun install                  # install dependencies
bun run dev                  # run the TUI from source
bun run src/index.tsx -p "task" --yolo   # headless one-shot (the e2e test entry)
bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit       # type check — must stay clean
bun run build                # regenerate logo + compile dist/glint
bun run install-bin          # install dist/glint to ~/.local/bin
```

All of these must keep working with no arguments and no manual setup. If your change affects any of them, rerun the affected one in the same session and prove it.

## Architecture (read before editing)

- `src/core/` — engine, no UI imports allowed here:
  - `groq.ts` streaming client (retries, SSE) · `protocol.ts` tool-block parsing (XML + sentinel forms)
  - `agent.ts` the loop: reasoning-channel salvage, turn-scoped dedup, reality/verification nudges
  - `tools.ts` tool registry · `prompts.ts` system prompt · `compact.ts` history compaction
  - `diagnostics.ts` hash-chained local JSONL traces · `logger.ts` file log · `session.ts`/`memory.ts`/`skills.ts` persistence
- `src/tui.tsx` + `src/components/` — Ink UI. Fullscreen alternate-screen layout: fixed `height={rows}` root, bottom-anchored transcript (`justifyContent="flex-end"` + `overflow="hidden"`), input + status welded to the bottom. No `<Static>`/native scrollback — PgUp/PgDn scrolls the in-app transcript. `startApp` enters/leaves the alt-screen buffer (`\x1b[?1049h/l`).
- `src/generated/logo.ts` — generated by `scripts/build-logo.ts` from `../embedme.html`. Never edit by hand.
- `src/headless.ts` — `-p` one-shot mode used for e2e testing.

## Hard-won constraints (violate these and the agent breaks)

1. **groq/compound has NO custom function calling.** Tools work via text blocks (`<glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool>`). The model drifts between formats — `protocol.ts` parses both XML and `<<<glint:tool` sentinel forms. Keep both.
2. **The model "executes" tools inside its reasoning channel.** `agent.ts` salvages calls from `res.reasoning`, deduped per turn (`turnExecuted`). Removing the dedup causes infinite re-execution loops; removing the salvage makes the agent claim work it never did.
3. **The model fabricates.** Three guards exist: the reality nudge (final answer claims actions, zero tools ran), the verification nudge (files modified, nothing run afterward), and premature-claim suppression (`claimsAction`). Test against fabrication explicitly after any prompt or loop change.
4. **Built-in compound tools must stay disabled in the agent loop** (`enabledTools: []`) or compound's server-side ReAct loop intercepts the conversation. Web access goes through the local `web_search` tool, which one-shots compound-mini WITH built-ins enabled.
5. **Non-zero bash exit must throw** (status: error) — silent failure re-enables fabricated success claims.
6. **The model leaks its base identity** ("I'm ChatGPT") and **describes files it never read**. The system prompt pins identity and bans assumption ("look first"); mid-round text longer than ~240 chars is held back as a draft answer. Keep both.
7. **Cost is computed from `usage_breakdown`** (compound is pass-through priced; `pricing.ts`). The streaming client must keep capturing `x_groq.usage_breakdown` from the final SSE chunk.

## Rules

- Real implementations only. No placeholders, no TODO stubs, no mock data presented as real.
- Type-check (`bunx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`) must pass clean before declaring done.
- Every engine change gets an e2e proof: run a headless task that exercises it and verify the filesystem outcome independently — do not trust the agent's own claims (see constraint 3).
- TUI changes get a tmux proof: launch in tmux, send keys, capture-pane, read the render.
- Keep `src/core/` free of UI imports; keep UI free of direct Groq calls.
- The API key and model names in `config.ts` are hardcoded by explicit project requirement; env `GROQ_API_KEY` overrides. Do not "fix" this.
- Logging is mandatory: every new event type goes through `logger.ts`, every agent-visible event also through `diagnostics.trace`.
- Diagnostics are local-only by design ("the most secure transport is no transport"). Never add a network sink.

## Final checklist

1. tsc clean.
2. Headless e2e run (simple + one failure-mode task) with filesystem-verified results.
3. TUI smoke test in tmux if UI was touched.
4. `bun run build` succeeds and `dist/glint --version` works if anything under `src/` changed.
5. No placeholder text, no dead code, no claims without proof.

---

# Playbook: Making a Weak Text-Only LLM (groq/compound) Produce Excellent Animated Websites Through Scaffolding Alone

The thesis holds, and there's strong evidence for *why*: Anthropic's own engineering team documented that even a frontier model (Claude), *without* design scaffolding, "produces the same purple-gradient, Inter-on-white, three-card-with-rounded-corners design repeatedly," and that a single skill file flips it to look "like it was made by an actual designer." The quality delta on frontend is dominated by the prompt, not the model. A weak model + the right scaffolding therefore closes most of the gap on this narrow domain. Below are the concrete techniques, ranked by impact, each pastable into a system prompt or skill file.

---

## TIER 1 — Highest impact: kill "AI slop" by banning defaults and forcing aesthetic commitment

This is the single biggest lever. The exact mechanism Anthropic ships in its frontend-design skill is: (1) name the failure mode, (2) ban specific defaults by name, (3) supply loaded aesthetic vocabulary, (4) force a committed choice *before* any code. Paste this block near-verbatim — it is Anthropic's own distilled aesthetics prompt:

```
<frontend_aesthetics>
You tend to converge toward generic, "on distribution" outputs. In frontend
design, this creates what users call the "AI slop" aesthetic. Avoid this: make
creative, distinctive frontends that surprise and delight. Focus on:

Typography: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid
generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices.

Color & Theme: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency.
Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes.
Draw from IDE themes and cultural aesthetics for inspiration.

Motion: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only
solutions. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with
staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered
micro-interactions.

Backgrounds: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors.
Layer CSS gradients, use geometric patterns, or add contextual effects.

Avoid generic AI-generated aesthetics:
- Overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts, Space Grotesk)
- Clichéd color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds)
- Predictable layouts and component patterns
- Cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character

Make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context.
</frontend_aesthetics>
```

Source: [Anthropic Claude Cookbook — Prompting for frontend aesthetics](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/coding-prompting-for-frontend-aesthetics).

**Commitment-forcing step** (critical for a weak model — it can't be trusted to "feel" its way to a direction): make the model emit a one-line design manifesto *before* writing any code. Provide named directions so it picks an extreme rather than the median:

> Before writing code, output exactly one line: `DIRECTION: <one of: Linear-style minimal-dark | editorial/serif | brutalist | neo-brutalist | glassmorphism | art-deco | luxury-dark | organic>`, plus the chosen font pairing and 3 hex color tokens. Then build to that direction with full commitment.

Named-aesthetic definitions to embed so the weak model has concrete targets (from [NN/g on neobrutalism](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/neobrutalism/), [Bejamas](https://bejamas.com/blog/neubrutalism-web-design-trend), [Wuko Media](https://wukomedia.com/blog/brutalism-skeuomorphism-or-glassmorphism-web-design/)):

- **Linear/Vercel-style:** dark canvas (#08090a–#0d0e10), near-white text, one saturated accent, system-ish but tight type, hairline 1px borders, generous whitespace, subtle gradient glows.
- **Glassmorphism:** semi-transparent panels, `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, 1px translucent white border, layered over a colorful/blurred background for depth.
- **Neo-brutalism:** thick black borders, hard offset box-shadows (no blur), flat saturated colors, bold sans, compartmentalized boxes, intentional grid-breaking.
- **Editorial:** large serif display (Playfair/Fraunces), high size contrast, asymmetric columns, restrained palette.

---

## TIER 2 — Inject an explicit design system (tokens) so the model never invents arbitrary values

A weak model produces inconsistent spacing/sizing. Hard-code the scales as CSS variables in the prompt and instruct it to use *only* these tokens. This is exactly what v0 does internally ("spacing systems: rhythmic layout patterns," "typography scales: harmonious text hierarchy," consistent border radii — [v0 system prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306)). 8px-base spacing and a modular type scale are the industry standard ([Designary](https://blog.designary.com/p/spacing-systems-and-scales-ui-design), [FontFYI type scale](https://fontfyi.com/blog/building-type-scale-design-system/)):

```css
:root{
  /* 8px spacing scale — use ONLY these */
  --s-1:4px; --s-2:8px; --s-3:12px; --s-4:16px; --s-6:24px;
  --s-8:32px; --s-12:48px; --s-16:64px; --s-24:96px; --s-32:128px;
  /* modular type scale (1.25 ratio) */
  --t-sm:.8rem; --t-base:1rem; --t-lg:1.25rem; --t-xl:1.563rem;
  --t-2xl:1.953rem; --t-3xl:2.441rem; --t-4xl:3.052rem; --t-5xl:3.815rem;
  /* tokens — fill per DIRECTION */
  --bg:#08090a; --surface:#111214; --text:#e6e6e6; --muted:#8a8f98;
  --accent:#5e6ad2; --border:rgba(255,255,255,.08); --radius:12px;
}
```

Typography rubric to enforce (Anthropic's isolated typography prompt — pastable):

> Never use: Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, system fonts. Pick from — code: JetBrains Mono / Fira Code; editorial: Playfair Display / Fraunces / Crimson Pro; startup: Clash Display / Satoshi / Cabinet Grotesque; technical: IBM Plex. Pairing principle: high contrast (display + mono, serif + geometric sans). Use weight extremes (100/200 vs 800/900, not 400 vs 600) and size jumps of 3x+, not 1.5x. Load from Google Fonts. State your choice before coding.

This converts vague taste into copy-pasteable rules a weak model can follow mechanically — the highest-leverage form of scaffolding.

---

## TIER 3 — Default animation toolkit, with canonical CDN snippets to embed

The cookbook's key insight for "wow per token": **one orchestrated staggered page-load reveal beats scattered micro-interactions.** Tell the model to default to that. Ranked by wow-per-token for a text-only model emitting a single HTML file:

**1. CSS-only staggered reveal (highest ROI — zero deps, always works).** Make this the *default*:
```css
@keyframes rise{from{opacity:0;transform:translateY(20px)}to{opacity:1;transform:none}}
.reveal{animation:rise .6s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) both}
.reveal:nth-child(1){animation-delay:.05s} .reveal:nth-child(2){animation-delay:.12s}
.reveal:nth-child(3){animation-delay:.19s} /* ...stagger via animation-delay */
```

**2. CSS scroll-driven animations** (no JS, reveal-on-scroll). Modern, Chromium + Firefox-flagged ([Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/css-ui/scroll-driven-animations), [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_scroll-driven_animations)):
```css
.card{animation:rise linear both; animation-timeline:view(); animation-range:entry 0% cover 30%;}
```

**3. GSAP + ScrollTrigger** — best wow-per-token for JS scroll work; the model knows it well. CDN + idiomatic snippets (verified via Context7 GSAP docs + [GSAP ScrollTrigger docs](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/Plugins/ScrollTrigger/)):
```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3.12.5/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3.12.5/dist/ScrollTrigger.min.js"></script>
<script>
gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);
// batch reveal-on-scroll with stagger (idiomatic):
ScrollTrigger.batch(".card",{onEnter:b=>gsap.to(b,{autoAlpha:1,y:0,stagger:.1})});
// pinned scrub section:
gsap.to(".panel",{xPercent:-100,ease:"none",
  scrollTrigger:{trigger:".wrap",pin:true,scrub:.5,end:"+=2000"}});
</script>
```

**4. Motion (motion.dev, the Motion One/Framer successor)** — clean ESM via CDN, great stagger ([motion.dev quick-start](https://motion.dev/docs/quick-start), [stagger](https://motion.dev/docs/stagger)):
```html
<script type="module">
import {animate,stagger,scroll} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/motion@latest/+esm";
animate("li",{opacity:[0,1],y:[20,0]},{delay:stagger(0.08)});
</script>
```
For React, the cookbook explicitly says: "Use Motion library for React when available" (`framer-motion` / `motion`).

**5. anime.js v4** — ESM via CDN ([animejs docs](https://animejs.com/documentation/getting-started/imports-old/)):
```html
<script type="module">
import {animate,stagger} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/animejs@4.0.0/+esm";
animate(".item",{translateY:[-20,0],opacity:[0,1],delay:stagger(100,{from:"center"}),duration:600});
</script>
```

**6. View Transitions API** — page/state transitions ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using)): same-doc `document.startViewTransition(()=>{/*update DOM*/})`; cross-doc just needs `@view-transition{navigation:auto;}` in CSS of both pages.

**Default rule for the prompt:** "Default to CSS-only staggered page-load reveals. If JS is allowed and scroll choreography is wanted, load GSAP+ScrollTrigger from the exact CDN tags above. Never hand-roll easing — use cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) or GSAP power eases."

---

## TIER 4 — Generate → self-critique → refine loop (a harness multiplier, not a prompt line)

This is where a weak model gains the most at runtime. **Self-Refine** (Madaan et al., 2023) shows a *single* LLM acting as generator → feedback-provider → refiner, with no training, yields **~20% absolute average improvement** across 7 tasks including code optimization — and explicitly states "even GPT-4 can be further improved at test time" ([arXiv 2303.17651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)). The gain is *larger* for weaker models because they leave more on the table in one pass.

For frontend specifically, the design-critique research shows the feedback must be **grounded and rubric-scored**: UICrit feeds the model a screenshot, has it emit critiques tied to regions/bounding boxes plus a **1–5 design-quality rating**, and iterative refinement of the critique improves specificity ([UICrit, arXiv 2407.08850](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.08850); [Visual Prompting w/ Iterative Refinement, arXiv 2412.16829](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16829)).

Harness recipe (works text-only, since groq/compound has no vision — critique the *code*, not a screenshot):

1. **Generate** the HTML to the design system + DIRECTION.
2. **Critique** with a forced design-critic persona and a numeric rubric, e.g.:
   > You are a senior product designer. Score the code 1–5 on each: (a) typography contrast & non-default fonts, (b) color cohesion & accent discipline, (c) spacing rhythm (are all values on the 8px scale?), (d) animation orchestration (is there one staggered load reveal?), (e) atmosphere/background depth, (f) layout interest (asymmetry/grid-breaking vs 3-card-row). For every score <4, give one concrete, line-level fix. End with the lowest score.
3. **Refine** by feeding the critique back: "Apply every fix where score <4. Output the full revised file."
4. **Loop** until min score ≥4 or 2–3 iterations (Self-Refine shows diminishing returns after ~2–3).

The rubric is what makes a *weak* model's self-critique useful: it can't generate good feedback freely, but it can grade against an explicit checklist and act on the failures.

---

## TIER 5 — Borrow the production tool conventions (v0 / bolt / lovable)

What the leaked scaffolds actually enforce — fold these constraints in:

- **bolt.new** (verbatim): *"For all designs I ask you to make, have them be beautiful, not cookie cutter. Make webpages that are fully featured and worthy for production."* Plus: JSX + Tailwind + React hooks + **Lucide React** for icons; *"Do not install other packages for UI themes, icons, etc unless absolutely necessary"*; use **Unsplash** stock photos by URL only (link, don't download). ([bolt prompt](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AntDX316/HF-Spaces/blob/main/.bolt/prompt), [x1xhlol leak repo](https://github.com/x1xhlol/system-prompts-and-models-of-ai-tools))
- **v0**: defaults to **shadcn/ui** + **Tailwind CSS variable–based color tokens**, **mobile-first responsive** required, **WCAG 2.1 compliance built-in** (semantic HTML + ARIA), **Framer Motion** for animation. ([v0 prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306), [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2024/Nov/25/leaked-system-prompts-from-vercel-v0/))
- **Common thread:** lean, opinionated stack + non-negotiable quality floors (responsive, accessible, production-worthy, no cookie-cutter). Lock the stack so the weak model never wanders.

Concrete constraints to add to the system prompt: *"Icons: Lucide only. Images: Unsplash URLs only. Must be mobile-first responsive and WCAG 2.1 (semantic HTML, ARIA labels, visible focus states). Use only the CSS variables defined above for color/spacing."*

---

## Suggested assembly order in the system prompt / skill file

1. The `<frontend_aesthetics>` slop-ban block (Tier 1).
2. Forced `DIRECTION:` manifesto line + named-aesthetic definitions (Tier 1).
3. Token CSS block + typography rubric (Tier 2).
4. Animation defaults + the exact CDN snippets (Tier 3).
5. Hard constraints: Lucide, Unsplash, responsive, WCAG, tokens-only (Tier 5).
6. In the harness loop, the rubric-scored critic persona + refine pass (Tier 4).

**Net:** Tiers 1–2 alone (banning defaults + injecting a token system + forcing a committed direction) capture most of the quality jump and cost only prompt tokens. Tier 4's critique loop is the runtime multiplier that disproportionately helps a weak model. Tier 3 supplies the "wow," and Tier 5 the production floor.

Key sources: [Anthropic frontend-aesthetics cookbook](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/coding-prompting-for-frontend-aesthetics), [Self-Refine (arXiv 2303.17651)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651), [UICrit (arXiv 2407.08850)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.08850), [v0 prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306), [bolt prompt](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AntDX316/HF-Spaces/blob/main/.bolt/prompt), [GSAP ScrollTrigger](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/Plugins/ScrollTrigger/), [motion.dev](https://motion.dev/docs/quick-start), [animejs](https://animejs.com/documentation/getting-started/installation/), [MDN scroll-driven animations](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_scroll-driven_animations), [MDN View Transitions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using).

---

# Playbook: Making a Weak Text-Only LLM (groq/compound) Produce Excellent Animated Websites Through Scaffolding Alone

The thesis holds, and there's strong evidence for *why*: Anthropic's own engineering team documented that even a frontier model (Claude), *without* design scaffolding, "produces the same purple-gradient, Inter-on-white, three-card-with-rounded-corners design repeatedly," and that a single skill file flips it to look "like it was made by an actual designer." The quality delta on frontend is dominated by the prompt, not the model. A weak model + the right scaffolding therefore closes most of the gap on this narrow domain. Below are the concrete techniques, ranked by impact, each pastable into a system prompt or skill file.

---

## TIER 1 — Highest impact: kill "AI slop" by banning defaults and forcing aesthetic commitment

This is the single biggest lever. The exact mechanism Anthropic ships in its frontend-design skill is: (1) name the failure mode, (2) ban specific defaults by name, (3) supply loaded aesthetic vocabulary, (4) force a committed choice *before* any code. Paste this block near-verbatim — it is Anthropic's own distilled aesthetics prompt:

```
<frontend_aesthetics>
You tend to converge toward generic, "on distribution" outputs. In frontend
design, this creates what users call the "AI slop" aesthetic. Avoid this: make
creative, distinctive frontends that surprise and delight. Focus on:

Typography: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid
generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices.

Color & Theme: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency.
Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes.
Draw from IDE themes and cultural aesthetics for inspiration.

Motion: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only
solutions. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with
staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered
micro-interactions.

Backgrounds: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors.
Layer CSS gradients, use geometric patterns, or add contextual effects.

Avoid generic AI-generated aesthetics:
- Overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts, Space Grotesk)
- Clichéd color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds)
- Predictable layouts and component patterns
- Cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character

Make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context.
</frontend_aesthetics>
```

Source: [Anthropic Claude Cookbook — Prompting for frontend aesthetics](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/coding-prompting-for-frontend-aesthetics).

**Commitment-forcing step** (critical for a weak model — it can't be trusted to "feel" its way to a direction): make the model emit a one-line design manifesto *before* writing any code. Provide named directions so it picks an extreme rather than the median:

> Before writing code, output exactly one line: `DIRECTION: <one of: Linear-style minimal-dark | editorial/serif | brutalist | neo-brutalist | glassmorphism | art-deco | luxury-dark | organic>`, plus the chosen font pairing and 3 hex color tokens. Then build to that direction with full commitment.

Named-aesthetic definitions to embed so the weak model has concrete targets (from [NN/g on neobrutalism](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/neobrutalism/), [Bejamas](https://bejamas.com/blog/neubrutalism-web-design-trend), [Wuko Media](https://wukomedia.com/blog/brutalism-skeuomorphism-or-glassmorphism-web-design/)):

- **Linear/Vercel-style:** dark canvas (#08090a–#0d0e10), near-white text, one saturated accent, system-ish but tight type, hairline 1px borders, generous whitespace, subtle gradient glows.
- **Glassmorphism:** semi-transparent panels, `backdrop-filter: blur(12px)`, 1px translucent white border, layered over a colorful/blurred background for depth.
- **Neo-brutalism:** thick black borders, hard offset box-shadows (no blur), flat saturated colors, bold sans, compartmentalized boxes, intentional grid-breaking.
- **Editorial:** large serif display (Playfair/Fraunces), high size contrast, asymmetric columns, restrained palette.

---

## TIER 2 — Inject an explicit design system (tokens) so the model never invents arbitrary values

A weak model produces inconsistent spacing/sizing. Hard-code the scales as CSS variables in the prompt and instruct it to use *only* these tokens. This is exactly what v0 does internally ("spacing systems: rhythmic layout patterns," "typography scales: harmonious text hierarchy," consistent border radii — [v0 system prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306)). 8px-base spacing and a modular type scale are the industry standard ([Designary](https://blog.designary.com/p/spacing-systems-and-scales-ui-design), [FontFYI type scale](https://fontfyi.com/blog/building-type-scale-design-system/)):

```css
:root{
  /* 8px spacing scale — use ONLY these */
  --s-1:4px; --s-2:8px; --s-3:12px; --s-4:16px; --s-6:24px;
  --s-8:32px; --s-12:48px; --s-16:64px; --s-24:96px; --s-32:128px;
  /* modular type scale (1.25 ratio) */
  --t-sm:.8rem; --t-base:1rem; --t-lg:1.25rem; --t-xl:1.563rem;
  --t-2xl:1.953rem; --t-3xl:2.441rem; --t-4xl:3.052rem; --t-5xl:3.815rem;
  /* tokens — fill per DIRECTION */
  --bg:#08090a; --surface:#111214; --text:#e6e6e6; --muted:#8a8f98;
  --accent:#5e6ad2; --border:rgba(255,255,255,.08); --radius:12px;
}
```

Typography rubric to enforce (Anthropic's isolated typography prompt — pastable):

> Never use: Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, system fonts. Pick from — code: JetBrains Mono / Fira Code; editorial: Playfair Display / Fraunces / Crimson Pro; startup: Clash Display / Satoshi / Cabinet Grotesque; technical: IBM Plex. Pairing principle: high contrast (display + mono, serif + geometric sans). Use weight extremes (100/200 vs 800/900, not 400 vs 600) and size jumps of 3x+, not 1.5x. Load from Google Fonts. State your choice before coding.

This converts vague taste into copy-pasteable rules a weak model can follow mechanically — the highest-leverage form of scaffolding.

---

## TIER 3 — Default animation toolkit, with canonical CDN snippets to embed

The cookbook's key insight for "wow per token": **one orchestrated staggered page-load reveal beats scattered micro-interactions.** Tell the model to default to that. Ranked by wow-per-token for a text-only model emitting a single HTML file:

**1. CSS-only staggered reveal (highest ROI — zero deps, always works).** Make this the *default*:
```css
@keyframes rise{from{opacity:0;transform:translateY(20px)}to{opacity:1;transform:none}}
.reveal{animation:rise .6s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) both}
.reveal:nth-child(1){animation-delay:.05s} .reveal:nth-child(2){animation-delay:.12s}
.reveal:nth-child(3){animation-delay:.19s} /* ...stagger via animation-delay */
```

**2. CSS scroll-driven animations** (no JS, reveal-on-scroll). Modern, Chromium + Firefox-flagged ([Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/css-ui/scroll-driven-animations), [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_scroll-driven_animations)):
```css
.card{animation:rise linear both; animation-timeline:view(); animation-range:entry 0% cover 30%;}
```

**3. GSAP + ScrollTrigger** — best wow-per-token for JS scroll work; the model knows it well. CDN + idiomatic snippets (verified via Context7 GSAP docs + [GSAP ScrollTrigger docs](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/Plugins/ScrollTrigger/)):
```html
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3.12.5/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3.12.5/dist/ScrollTrigger.min.js"></script>
<script>
gsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);
// batch reveal-on-scroll with stagger (idiomatic):
ScrollTrigger.batch(".card",{onEnter:b=>gsap.to(b,{autoAlpha:1,y:0,stagger:.1})});
// pinned scrub section:
gsap.to(".panel",{xPercent:-100,ease:"none",
  scrollTrigger:{trigger:".wrap",pin:true,scrub:.5,end:"+=2000"}});
</script>
```

**4. Motion (motion.dev, the Motion One/Framer successor)** — clean ESM via CDN, great stagger ([motion.dev quick-start](https://motion.dev/docs/quick-start), [stagger](https://motion.dev/docs/stagger)):
```html
<script type="module">
import {animate,stagger,scroll} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/motion@latest/+esm";
animate("li",{opacity:[0,1],y:[20,0]},{delay:stagger(0.08)});
</script>
```
For React, the cookbook explicitly says: "Use Motion library for React when available" (`framer-motion` / `motion`).

**5. anime.js v4** — ESM via CDN ([animejs docs](https://animejs.com/documentation/getting-started/imports-old/)):
```html
<script type="module">
import {animate,stagger} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/animejs@4.0.0/+esm";
animate(".item",{translateY:[-20,0],opacity:[0,1],delay:stagger(100,{from:"center"}),duration:600});
</script>
```

**6. View Transitions API** — page/state transitions ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using)): same-doc `document.startViewTransition(()=>{/*update DOM*/})`; cross-doc just needs `@view-transition{navigation:auto;}` in CSS of both pages.

**Default rule for the prompt:** "Default to CSS-only staggered page-load reveals. If JS is allowed and scroll choreography is wanted, load GSAP+ScrollTrigger from the exact CDN tags above. Never hand-roll easing — use cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1) or GSAP power eases."

---

## TIER 4 — Generate → self-critique → refine loop (a harness multiplier, not a prompt line)

This is where a weak model gains the most at runtime. **Self-Refine** (Madaan et al., 2023) shows a *single* LLM acting as generator → feedback-provider → refiner, with no training, yields **~20% absolute average improvement** across 7 tasks including code optimization — and explicitly states "even GPT-4 can be further improved at test time" ([arXiv 2303.17651](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)). The gain is *larger* for weaker models because they leave more on the table in one pass.

For frontend specifically, the design-critique research shows the feedback must be **grounded and rubric-scored**: UICrit feeds the model a screenshot, has it emit critiques tied to regions/bounding boxes plus a **1–5 design-quality rating**, and iterative refinement of the critique improves specificity ([UICrit, arXiv 2407.08850](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.08850); [Visual Prompting w/ Iterative Refinement, arXiv 2412.16829](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16829)).

Harness recipe (works text-only, since groq/compound has no vision — critique the *code*, not a screenshot):

1. **Generate** the HTML to the design system + DIRECTION.
2. **Critique** with a forced design-critic persona and a numeric rubric, e.g.:
   > You are a senior product designer. Score the code 1–5 on each: (a) typography contrast & non-default fonts, (b) color cohesion & accent discipline, (c) spacing rhythm (are all values on the 8px scale?), (d) animation orchestration (is there one staggered load reveal?), (e) atmosphere/background depth, (f) layout interest (asymmetry/grid-breaking vs 3-card-row). For every score <4, give one concrete, line-level fix. End with the lowest score.
3. **Refine** by feeding the critique back: "Apply every fix where score <4. Output the full revised file."
4. **Loop** until min score ≥4 or 2–3 iterations (Self-Refine shows diminishing returns after ~2–3).

The rubric is what makes a *weak* model's self-critique useful: it can't generate good feedback freely, but it can grade against an explicit checklist and act on the failures.

---

## TIER 5 — Borrow the production tool conventions (v0 / bolt / lovable)

What the leaked scaffolds actually enforce — fold these constraints in:

- **bolt.new** (verbatim): *"For all designs I ask you to make, have them be beautiful, not cookie cutter. Make webpages that are fully featured and worthy for production."* Plus: JSX + Tailwind + React hooks + **Lucide React** for icons; *"Do not install other packages for UI themes, icons, etc unless absolutely necessary"*; use **Unsplash** stock photos by URL only (link, don't download). ([bolt prompt](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AntDX316/HF-Spaces/blob/main/.bolt/prompt), [x1xhlol leak repo](https://github.com/x1xhlol/system-prompts-and-models-of-ai-tools))
- **v0**: defaults to **shadcn/ui** + **Tailwind CSS variable–based color tokens**, **mobile-first responsive** required, **WCAG 2.1 compliance built-in** (semantic HTML + ARIA), **Framer Motion** for animation. ([v0 prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306), [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2024/Nov/25/leaked-system-prompts-from-vercel-v0/))
- **Common thread:** lean, opinionated stack + non-negotiable quality floors (responsive, accessible, production-worthy, no cookie-cutter). Lock the stack so the weak model never wanders.

Concrete constraints to add to the system prompt: *"Icons: Lucide only. Images: Unsplash URLs only. Must be mobile-first responsive and WCAG 2.1 (semantic HTML, ARIA labels, visible focus states). Use only the CSS variables defined above for color/spacing."*

---

## Suggested assembly order in the system prompt / skill file

1. The `<frontend_aesthetics>` slop-ban block (Tier 1).
2. Forced `DIRECTION:` manifesto line + named-aesthetic definitions (Tier 1).
3. Token CSS block + typography rubric (Tier 2).
4. Animation defaults + the exact CDN snippets (Tier 3).
5. Hard constraints: Lucide, Unsplash, responsive, WCAG, tokens-only (Tier 5).
6. In the harness loop, the rubric-scored critic persona + refine pass (Tier 4).

**Net:** Tiers 1–2 alone (banning defaults + injecting a token system + forcing a committed direction) capture most of the quality jump and cost only prompt tokens. Tier 4's critique loop is the runtime multiplier that disproportionately helps a weak model. Tier 3 supplies the "wow," and Tier 5 the production floor.

Key sources: [Anthropic frontend-aesthetics cookbook](https://platform.claude.com/cookbook/coding-prompting-for-frontend-aesthetics), [Self-Refine (arXiv 2303.17651)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651), [UICrit (arXiv 2407.08850)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.08850), [v0 prompt](https://agentic-design.ai/prompt-hub/vercel/v0-20250306), [bolt prompt](https://huggingface.co/spaces/AntDX316/HF-Spaces/blob/main/.bolt/prompt), [GSAP ScrollTrigger](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/Plugins/ScrollTrigger/), [motion.dev](https://motion.dev/docs/quick-start), [animejs](https://animejs.com/documentation/getting-started/installation/), [MDN scroll-driven animations](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_scroll-driven_animations), [MDN View Transitions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using).

# Implementation Plan: Better Animated Websites in glint-cli

## Recommended architecture decision (the key question)

**Use a hybrid: a lazy-loaded, bundled "frontend design" knowledge block gated by frontend-intent detection, injected as ONE system-prompt section — NOT an always-on section and NOT the user-skill mechanism.**

Reasoning, ranked by the constraint "lowest complexity, non-frontend tasks unaffected":

- **Always-on system prompt** — rejected. The design block (rubric + tokens + CDN snippets + manifesto step) is 1.5–3 KB. Adding it to every request bloats a text-only model's prompt for backend bug fixes and violates the spirit of constraint 6 (keep the prompt lean so the model doesn't drift). Also pollutes subagents.
- **User-skill mechanism (`~/.glint/skills`)** — rejected as the primary path. Skills only inject `name + description` into the prompt (prompts.ts:107); the body only enters context when the user explicitly types `/name`. So a skill cannot passively influence "build me a landing page" unless the user knows to invoke it. There's no bundled-skill loader, and adding one is more code than a gated prompt section.
- **Frontend-intent-gated bundled section** — chosen. A pure string constant lives in a new core module; `buildSystemPrompt` appends it only when the turn's user message matches a frontend-intent regex. Zero new files in `~/.glint`, zero new tools required for A, inert for backend tasks by construction, never added for subagents.

The intent signal is computed in `runTurn` (it already has `userMessage`) and threaded into `buildSystemPrompt` via a new opt. This same boolean gates B and C, so all three share one detector.

---

     description: "Statically check an HTML/CSS file for design/animation deficiencies (hardcoded colors, ad-hoc font sizes, missing scroll-reveal, missing prefers-reduced-motion, no animation). Returns a list of fixable issues.",

Confirmed: JSON key ordering makes the dedup key unstable. I now have everything I need with empirical evidence. Here is the audit.

---

# Glint tool-use reliability audit

Static robustness review of the text tool-call mechanism. Evidence is `file:line`; parser claims are empirically verified (see notes). Ranked most-frequent/most-damaging first.

## TL;DR severity ranking

| # | Failure mode | Frequency for weak model | Damage |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `write_file`/`edit_file` args break the JSON parser (literal newlines, unescaped quotes) | **Very frequent** | Severe — silent no-op, fabrication follows |
| 2 | `edit_file` exact-match misses (whitespace/paraphrase) | **Very frequent** | High — repeated failure, blind retries |
| 3 | Lenient parser fails on trailing commas / single quotes | Frequent | Severe — silent drop |
| 4 | maxTokens cuts a tool block mid-emit | Frequent on big writes | Severe — silent drop + fabrication |
| 5 | Reasoning-channel dedup drops legitimate repeat calls | Frequent | High — second edit/read silently skipped |
| 6 | Dedup key unstable under JSON key reordering | Occasional | Medium — re-execution / loops |
| 7 | Silently dropped block → no error signal to model | Frequent (consequence of 1–4) | High — model can't self-correct |
| 8 | Compaction drops tool results model still needs | Occasional | Medium |
| 9 | `visiblePrefix` leaks/garbles sentinel partials; SSE `\r\n` | Edge | Low–Medium |

---

## 1. `write_file`/`edit_file` args break the parser — literal newlines & unescaped quotes (MOST DAMAGING)

`parseJsonLenient` (protocol.ts:66-105) is plain `JSON.parse` plus a brace-balancing fallback. Both require **strict JSON string escaping**. A weak model emitting code in a `content`/`new_string` arg almost never escapes correctly. Empirically verified:

- **Literal newlines in `content`** → `FAIL` (parse returns null). JSON forbids raw newlines in strings; the model writes real line breaks in a code blob.
- **Unescaped `"` in content** (e.g. HTML `<div class="x">`) → `FAIL`. Closes the string early; brace-balancer then miscounts.
- Properly escaped `\n` and `\"` → parse OK. So correctness hinges entirely on the model escaping every newline and quote inside a multi-line code payload — exactly what groq/compound is worst at.

This is the dominant break for `edit_file`/`write_file` specifically, because those are the only tools whose args routinely carry large code with braces, quotes, and newlines. When it fails, `parseToolCalls` returns `[]` (protocol.ts:26 guard), the loop sees `calls.length === 0` (agent.ts:276), and the write **silently never happens** — then the reality/verify nudges fire or the model fabricates success.

**Fix (high impact, minimal):** stop forcing code through JSON string-escaping. Add a raw-payload escape hatch the model can use for the big arg. Concretely, support a fenced body form in `parseJsonLenient`: parse the JSON object for everything *except* a designated content field delivered as a trailing fenced block, e.g.

```
<glint:tool>
{"tool":"write_file","args":{"path":"a.py"}}
---content---
def f():
    return 1
---end---
</glint:tool>
```

When `---content---` is present, take its raw text verbatim as `args.content` (or `args.new_string`) — no escaping required. Document this in prompts.ts:53-70 as the *preferred* form for write/edit. This removes the single largest source of silent tool loss. (Keep strict-JSON parsing as the path for small args.)

A cheaper partial mitigation: in `parseJsonLenient`, before giving up, retry with a "raw string-value rescue" that re-escapes literal newlines/tabs inside the value region. But the fenced escape hatch is far more robust for a weak model.

## 2. `edit_file` exact-string match is too brittle (VERY FREQUENT)

tools.ts:146 `content.split(oldStr).length - 1` — pure byte-exact match. A weak model reconstructing `old_string` from memory will routinely miss on:
- leading/trailing whitespace and indentation (tabs vs spaces),
- trailing whitespace on a line,
- paraphrased or reflowed lines.

The error guidance (tools.ts:147-160) is decent — it shows nearby partial-match lines and tells the model to re-read or fall back to `write_file`. But for a weak model this still means many wasted rounds, and the nearby-match heuristic only triggers when `firstLine.length > 3` and the first 30 chars happen to substring-match (tools.ts:153).

**Fix (high impact):** add tolerant matching before declaring failure:
1. **Whitespace-normalized fallback:** if exact `count === 0`, retry matching with each line's leading/trailing whitespace stripped for *locating* the region, then replace the original (un-normalized) span. This alone kills the most common (indentation) miss.
2. **Unique-line-anchor / line-range edit:** accept an optional `{start_line, end_line}` form so the model can edit by location instead of reproducing exact bytes.
3. The existing "rewrite whole file with write_file" fallback (tools.ts:159, prompts.ts:70) is the right escape hatch — but it only helps if `write_file` itself parses, which loops back to failure mode #1. Fix #1 first.

Keep the exact path as default; add normalized matching as the automatic second attempt.

## 3. Lenient parser rejects trailing commas and single quotes (FREQUENT silent drop)

Verified `FAIL`:
- **Trailing comma**: `{"path":"a.ts",}` → null. Common weak-model output.
- **Single-quoted keys/strings**: `{'tool':'read_file',...}` → null. The brace-balancer (protocol.ts:79-101) only special-cases `"` for in-string detection, so single-quote JSON never recovers.

Both currently cause silent total loss of the call.

**Fix (minimal):** in `parseJsonLenient`, before the final `JSON.parse(cleaned.slice(...))`, run two cheap normalizations on the extracted object span:
- strip trailing commas: `s.replace(/,(\s*[}\]])/g, "$1")`
- if strict parse fails, attempt single→double quote conversion (guarded: only when no double quotes present, to avoid corrupting escaped content).
Then retry parse. Low risk, recovers a large class of weak-model JSON.

## 4. maxTokens truncates a tool block mid-emit (FREQUENT on large writes, SEVERE)

`DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS = 8192` (groq.ts:31), used for every agent round (agent.ts:253). A large `write_file` content blob can hit the cap before `</glint:tool>` is emitted. `XML_RE` (protocol.ts:18) is non-greedy and requires a closing `</glint:tool>`; with no close, **the whole block fails to match and is silently dropped**. The stream simply ends (groq.ts:116-118 `done`), no finish_reason check.

- **Re-reading the same file** after a change to confirm — dropped.

---end---

# Reliable Agentic Loops for a Weak Model: A glint Playbook

## The core thesis (what the evidence says)

Reliability for a weak model is **not** about smarter generation — it's about constraining the search space and catching errors before they compound. Three findings dominate:

1. **Errors compound super-linearly.** Aggregate pass@1 drops 76.3% → 52.1% from short to very-long tasks because errors are *positively correlated* — a weak model that takes a wrong turn persists in it. Qwen3-30B (a fair stand-in for compound's tier) scored **22.2% vs a 33.0% geometric prediction** — it fails 1.5× faster than chance would predict. ([Beyond pass@1](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29231v1))

2. **Decomposition + restart is the single highest-leverage fix.** Cutting a long task into segments and restarting the agent at boundaries gave Qwen3-30B **+41.5 pp** (34.3% → 75.8%). This is the biggest single number in the whole literature and it's pure harness work. ([Beyond pass@1](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29231v1))

3. **Memory scaffolds universally hurt long-horizon reliability** — all 10 models tested showed neutral-to-negative effects. Naive episodic memory should not be a default. ([Beyond pass@1](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29231v1); [terminal-agent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05344))

The throughline: glint's loop is **reactive** (nudges fire only on an empty final answer) and **flat** (one undifferentiated sequence of up to N rounds with no checkpoints, no plan, no loop detection). The wins come from making it **proactive** and **segmented**.

---

On a coding agent, N parallel *trajectories* are far costlier than N CoT samples. **Only** worth it for a single high-stakes, self-contained decision (e.g. the *plan* in #1, or a tricky algorithm), and even then use **Adaptive-Consistency** — sample until a lightweight confidence threshold, stop early — rather than a fixed N. ([Adaptive-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.11860)). Given glint's free-tier rate-limit reality, this ranks last.

---

## Failure-taxonomy → fix map

The MAST/terminal taxonomies cluster agent failures into **(a) system-design issues** (bad task routing, no error handling), **(b) inter-agent misalignment**, and **(c) task-verification failures** (inadequate output validation). ([Failure taxonomy](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.29231v1) refs MAST; [4-layer taxonomy](https://cobusgreyling.substack.com/p/the-four-layer-agent-failure-taxonomy))

| Failure class | glint exposure | Playbook fix |
|---|---|---|
| Missing-step / no plan | plan is optional prose | **#1** forced plan |
| Error compounding over horizon | flat loop, no checkpoints | **#2** segment + restart |
| Inadequate output validation | verification is reactive-only | **#3** proactive verify, **#6** reviewGoal gate |
| Incoherent looping / thrash | no loop detection at all | **#4** MOP-style detector + escalation |
| Instruction fade-out | goal stated once | **#5** periodic re-statement |
| Premature/false success claim | partially handled (failure nudge) | **#3 + #6** make it proactive |

---

## Recommended build order

1. **#1 forced plan + #4 loop detection** — highest impact, lowest cost, both reuse existing data (`turnExecuted`, `todo_write`). Do these first.
2. **#3 proactive verification** + **#6 wire reviewGoal** — flip glint from reactive to proactive; #6 is nearly free (code exists).
3. **#2 segment-and-restart** — the +41.5 pp move, but needs todo-driven compaction plumbing (medium effort).
4. **#5 goal re-statement + output summarization** — polish for long runs.
5. **#7 self-consistency** — only on the plan step, adaptive, if rate limits allow.

**One explicit anti-recommendation:** do **not** lean on episodic/cross-session memory as a reliability lever — the strongest long-horizon study found it neutral-to-harmful across every model tested.

- `src/core/compact.ts` — drive `compactHistory` off todo-completion, not only the 90k threshold (L7).
- `src/core/groq.ts` — expose per-call `temperature` override for the #4 escalation step (already plumbed via `ChatOptions`, just unused in `runTurn`).

# Prompt-Engineering Upgrades for glint's System Prompt + Loop

Goal: lift weak text-only `groq/compound` toward strong agentic reliability via scaffolding alone. Ranked by expected reliability impact for this specific model's failure modes. Each item notes evidence, glint's current state, and exact pastable text.

Grounding done: read `/home/lane/GR/glint-cli/src/core/prompts.ts` (full system prompt, tool-protocol section, single worked example) and `/home/lane/GR/glint-cli/src/core/agent.ts` (the loop, salvage, five reactive nudges).

---

## RANK 1 — Add MORE and MORE-DIVERSE few-shot examples (format adherence)

The single highest-leverage change. glint has exactly ONE worked example (a read→edit→done happy path). Weak models anchor format from examples far more than from spec prose; 2–10 diverse examples substantially improve format reliability, and a single example cannot demonstrate the cases where the model actually drifts.

- **Evidence:** Few-shot anchors output format; 2–3 examples already give large gains over zero/one-shot, and "reinforced format reminders minimize context drift" ([learnprompting](https://learnprompting.org/docs/basics/few_shot), [IBM](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/few-shot-prompting), [DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/few-shot-prompting)). For weak models specifically, format compliance is the weak point and "additional safeguards beyond a single example are necessary."
- **glint status:** MISSING — only one example, and it does not cover the model's actual failure modes (multiple parallel calls, a tool *error* + recovery, a pure-conversation no-tool turn, a web_search).
- **Exact text to add** after the existing example in the `## Tool protocol` section:

```
More examples (study the SHAPE, not the content):

Multiple independent reads in one message (they run in order):
[you]: Checking both config files.
<glint:tool>
{"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "package.json"}}
</glint:tool>
<glint:tool>
{"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "tsconfig.json"}}
</glint:tool>

Recovering from a tool error (do NOT claim success — fix it):
[next message delivers]: <glint:result n="1" tool="edit_file" status="error"> old_string not found in file </glint:result>
[you]: The edit target moved. Re-reading the file to get the exact bytes.
<glint:tool>
{"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "config.json"}}
</glint:tool>

A question that needs no tools — answer in plain text, emit NO block:
[user]: what does this CLI do?
[you]: glint is a terminal coding agent. Ask it to read, edit, or run things and it acts on your machine directly.

WRONG — never do this (writing the result yourself, then continuing as if it ran):
[you]: <glint:tool>{"tool":"bash","args":{"command":"ls"}}</glint:tool>
Output: file1.ts file2.ts        ← FABRICATION. You did not run anything yet. END after the block and WAIT.
```

The explicit WRONG/negative example is itself an evidence-backed technique (showing failure cases) — see Rank 4.

---

## RANK 2 — Separate the reasoning step from the format step (tame the reasoning channel)

compound's worst failure is "acting inside the reasoning channel." The research-backed reason: **format restrictions degrade reasoning**, and the fix is to let the model reason freely first, THEN emit the constrained format as a distinct, final act. glint currently asks the model to reason and emit the JSON tool block together; this collides exactly with the documented failure mode.

- **Evidence:** "Let Me Speak Freely?" — significant decline in reasoning under format restrictions, worse with stricter constraints; recommended mitigation is to decouple reasoning from format conversion ([arXiv 2408.02442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442)). ReAct formalizes interleaved *thought → action → observation*, separating reasoning space from a clean action ([arXiv 2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03629), [promptingguide](https://www.promptingguide.ai/techniques/react)).
- **glint status:** PARTIALLY — the loop *salvages* reasoning-channel calls (good defense) but the prompt never teaches the model the correct division of labor. It treats reasoning as a leak to mop up rather than a place to think.
- **Exact text to add** to `## Tool protocol`, right before "CRITICAL rules":

```
Think first, then act — keep them separate. Use your reasoning to PLAN (which tool, what args, why). But a tool only runs when its block appears in your VISIBLE message and your message ENDS. Reasoning about a tool is not calling it; describing its output in your reasoning is not running it. So: think it through, then write ONE visible plain line + the tool block(s), then stop.
```

This reframes the reasoning channel as productive planning while making the visible block the only thing that counts — directly addressing constraint 2 in AGENTS.md at the prompt level instead of only the loop level.

---

## RANK 3 — Move identity + the 3 most critical rules to BOTH the top AND a closing reminder block (placement / repetition)

glint's prompt is long (~110 lines assembled) and the order is identity → env → protocol → effort → working style → project → memory → skills. The critical anti-fabrication and format rules sit in the MIDDLE, exactly where attention is weakest, and nothing is repeated at the end. The conversation also grows, pushing the system prompt further from the action point each round.

- **Evidence:** Lost-in-the-middle — models attend most to the START and END; reinforcement strategy is "identity/safety at top (primacy), reminders at bottom (recency) for double reinforcement" ([IntuitionLabs](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/llm-position-bias-primacy-recency-effects), [arXiv 2510.10276](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.10276)). Reasoning degradation begins ~3000 tokens, well under the window ([Grit Daily](https://gritdaily.com/impact-prompt-length-llm-performance/)).
- **glint status:** PARTIALLY — identity is correctly at the top; nothing is repeated at the end, and critical rules are mid-prompt.
- **Exact text to add** as the FINAL section (last `sections.push`, after skills, so it lands at the very end every round):

```
## Before you respond — the three rules that matter most
1. FORMAT: a tool runs only as a <glint:tool>{json}</glint:tool> block in your visible message; end the message right after it.
2. NO FABRICATION: never describe a result you have not received. If you claim you did X, a matching ok result must already exist above. No result = it did not happen.
3. LOOK, DON'T GUESS: never describe a file/project/system you did not read this conversation. Read it or omit it.
You are Glint, by Glint Research — not ChatGPT, not made by OpenAI.
```

---

## RANK 4 — Anti-fabrication: add NEGATIVE examples + a "cite the result n=" rule (proactive, not just reactive)

glint's three fabrication guards (`agent.ts` reality/verify/failure nudges) are all *reactive* — they fire after the model already fabricated. Research says the strongest prompt-side lever is making answers *auditable*: require the model to cite the supporting tool result before concluding, and show negative examples of fabrication.

- **Evidence:** "Make responses auditable — cite quotes/sources for each claim, retract if no quote can be found"; "inject 'do not present speculation as fact', require labels like [Unverified]"; "explicit citation slots sharply cut fabrication" ([MachineLearningMastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/7-prompt-engineering-tricks-to-mitigate-hallucinations-in-llms/), [Claude API docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations), [MDPI citation-enforced RAG](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/6/3013)). glint's `<glint:result n="N">` tags are a ready-made citation handle.
- **glint status:** MISSING the proactive citation requirement; the negative-example for fabrication is covered if you add the WRONG block from Rank 1.
- **Exact text to add** to `## Working style` (replace/augment the existing anti-assume bullet):

```
- Cite your evidence. When your final answer states a fact about the code, a file's contents, or a command's outcome, it must trace to a specific <glint:result n="N"> you received this turn. If you cannot point to the n= that proves a claim, you may not make the claim — read/run to get it, or say "I have not verified this." Quote the relevant line of tool output before drawing a conclusion from it.
```

This turns the existing `n=` result numbering into an enforceable grounding contract.

---

## RANK 5 — Add a lightweight Plan-and-Solve / step-back framing for higher-effort tasks (CoT that helps weak models)

Plain "think step by step" CoT *hurts* sub-~100B models (illogical chains → worse than no CoT). What lifts weaker models is *structured* reasoning: Plan-and-Solve (devise a plan, then execute) matches 8-shot CoT zero-shot, and step-back (abstract the principle first) gives +7–27% on reasoning tasks and is model-agnostic.

- **Evidence:** CoT only helps ~100B+ models; smaller models "wrote illogical chains → worse accuracy" ([arXiv 2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11903), [cameronrwolfe](https://cameronrwolfe.substack.com/p/chain-of-thought-prompting-for-llms)). Plan-and-Solve beats zero-shot-CoT "by a large margin," comparable to 8-shot CoT ([arXiv 2305.04091](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.04091)). Step-back: +7–27%, model-agnostic ([arXiv 2310.06117](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06117)).
- **glint status:** PARTIALLY — per-effort `effort.hint` exists but (per the code) is a generic hint, not a Plan-and-Solve scaffold. Recommend wiring this into the high/ultra effort hints in `config.ts` rather than the always-on prompt, to avoid bloating low-effort turns.
- **Exact text** for the high-effort hint:

```
For this task: first restate the goal in one line and list the concrete sub-steps you'll take (the plan). Then execute the plan one tool at a time, checking each result against the plan before the next step. If a result contradicts the plan, revise the plan — don't push ahead.
```

Keep `effort.hint` for low-effort SHORT (do not add planning overhead to trivial tasks — see Rank 6).

---

## RANK 6 — Tighten the prompt: dedupe, group, and gate verbosity by effort (conciseness vs thoroughness)

Long prompts measurably hurt weak models — reasoning degrades around ~3000 tokens and models "fail to follow extended instructions" and "struggle to filter irrelevant info." glint's `## Working style` has 11 dense bullets, several overlapping with the protocol's CRITICAL rules (fabrication is stated 3+ times across sections, verification twice). Redundancy is good *only when placed at start/end* (Rank 3); scattered mid-prompt repetition is just dilution.

- **Evidence:** "More words, less accuracy"; degradation ~3000 tokens, well below window; "extra details reduce accuracy, coherence, relevance; models can't filter irrelevant info" ([Grit Daily](https://gritdaily.com/impact-prompt-length-llm-performance/), [PromptLayer](https://blog.promptlayer.com/disadvantage-of-long-prompt-for-llm/), [MLOps Community](https://mlops.community/blog/the-impact-of-prompt-bloat-on-llm-output-quality)).
- **glint status:** MISSING — prompt has grown organically; no dedup, no effort-gating of verbosity.
- **Concrete actions** (not new prose — structural edits to `prompts.ts`):
  1. Consolidate the scattered fabrication statements into ONE place (the protocol CRITICAL rules) plus the closing reminder (Rank 3). Remove the duplicate fabrication/verification lines from `## Working style`.
  2. Convert `## Working style` from 11 bullets to ~6, leading with the action-shaping ones (concise, real changes, verify, fix-don't-retry, honest-failure).
  3. Gate the planning/thoroughness language behind effort (Rank 5) so low-effort turns stay lean.
  Net target: keep the always-on system prompt tight, push depth into the effort hint and into the start/end reinforcement rather than the middle.

---

## RANK 7 — Reinforce identity once more at the boundary (persona stability)

Persona instructions in the system prompt do shape stated identity, but they are fragile across turns/long contexts — which is why the recency-position reminder (Rank 3, last line) matters more than adding new identity prose at the top, where glint already pins it well.

- **Evidence:** Persona/system-prompt identity is established but exploitable/driftable across turns; defenses rely on keeping the persona rule *enforced across the session*, not just stated once ([arXiv 2507.22171](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22171), [SentinelOne](https://www.sentinelone.com/cybersecurity-101/data-and-ai/jailbreaking-llms/)).
- **glint status:** GOOD at top of prompt; the only gap is end-of-prompt recency reinforcement, already covered by the last line of the Rank 3 block. No separate change needed — just don't drop that line.

---

## Summary table

| # | Upgrade | glint status | Where |
|---|---------|-------------|-------|
| 1 | More/diverse few-shot examples (+ negative example) | MISSING | `prompts.ts` tool-protocol |
| 2 | Think-first-then-act separation framing | PARTIAL (loop only) | `prompts.ts` tool-protocol |
| 3 | Critical rules at START *and* END | PARTIAL (top only) | `prompts.ts` final section |
| 4 | Proactive "cite the result n=" grounding | MISSING | `prompts.ts` working style |
| 5 | Plan-and-Solve / step-back for high effort | PARTIAL (generic hint) | `config.ts` effort hints |
| 6 | Dedupe + effort-gate verbosity | MISSING | `prompts.ts` structure |
| 7 | End-of-prompt identity reinforcement | covered by #3 | — |

**Biggest wins for the stated goal (general reliability, beat Fable via scaffolding):** Ranks 1, 2, 3 — they target compound's three documented failure modes (format drift, reasoning-channel acting, mid-prompt rule decay) with the best-evidenced techniques, and all are pure prompt edits with no loop/model/key changes. Ranks 4–6 compound the gains and are low-risk. The most important caveat from the evidence is the tension between Rank 1 (add examples) and Rank 6 (prompts shouldn't bloat) — resolve it by gating depth behind effort and keeping the always-on core tight while reinforcing only the 3 critical rules at the end.

Sources: [Let Me Speak Freely (2408.02442)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442) · [Plan-and-Solve (2305.04091)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04091) · [Step-Back (2310.06117)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06117) · [CoT (2201.11903)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11903) · [ReAct (2210.03629)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03629) · [Lost in the Middle / position bias](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/llm-position-bias-primacy-recency-effects) · [Prompt length degradation](https://gritdaily.com/impact-prompt-length-llm-performance/) · [Few-shot](https://learnprompting.org/docs/basics/few_shot) · [Hallucination prompt tricks](https://machinelearningmastery.com/7-prompt-engineering-tricks-to-mitigate-hallucinations-in-llms/) · [Claude reduce-hallucinations docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations) · [Persona stability/jailbreak (2507.22171)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22171)

Three audits back, empirical runner still going (running real tasks — slow). Findings converge hard. The single root cause behind "sucks at basic tool use":

## The core bug: silent tool-call loss → fabrication cascade

`write_file`/`edit_file` carry code with newlines + quotes + braces. The weak model rarely JSON-escapes them right. `parseJsonLenient` (protocol.ts:66) returns null → `parseToolCalls` returns `[]` → loop sees "zero calls" (agent.ts:276) → write **silently never happened** → model thinks it never tried (nudges say "you ran zero tools", not "your block was malformed") → retries same broken escaping OR fabricates success. This one failure explains most of the "stupidity." Verified empirically by the audit agent (literal newline → FAIL, unescaped `"` → FAIL, trailing comma → FAIL, single quotes → FAIL).

## Unified fix plan, ranked by impact ÷ cost

**Tier 0 — tool-use reliability (fixes "basic tool use fails"):**
1. **Fenced raw-content escape hatch** for write/edit — payload after `---content---` taken verbatim, no JSON escaping. Kills the #1 silent-drop. (protocol.ts + prompts.ts)
2. **"Block detected but unparsed" feedback** — if `<glint:tool>` appears but parse yields 0 calls, tell the model *why* (unescaped quote/newline/trailing comma) instead of "you ran zero tools." (agent.ts:263)
3. **Trailing-comma + single-quote tolerance** in parser. (protocol.ts)
4. **Whitespace-normalized `edit_file` fallback** match before failing. (tools.ts:146)
5. **Canonicalize dedup key** (`JSON.stringify(args, sortedKeys)`) — fixes re-execution loops from key reordering. (agent.ts:261)
6. **Catch `finish_reason:"length"`** mid-block → tell model to split the write. (groq.ts)

**Tier 1 — loop reliability (fixes "gives up / thrashes / fabricates"):**
7. **Wire `reviewGoal` as completion gate** — it's fully built (agent.ts:144) and *never called*. Free win.
8. **Loop/thrash detection** — `turnExecuted` data already there, unused. Same call 3× → force different approach / temp bump.
9. **Proactive verification** — move guards out of the `calls.length===0` block so they fire *after* a risky edit, not only at the end.
10. **Forced plan-first step** on medium+ effort (Plan-and-Solve: biggest documented weak-model gain; segment+restart = +41.5pp in the literature).

**Tier 2 — prompt scaffolding (cheap, pure text):**
11. **More + diverse few-shot** (currently only 1 example) incl. a **negative/WRONG fabrication example** and a multi-call example.
12. **Think-first-then-act framing** — tames the reasoning-channel acting (compound's worst habit).
13. **Critical-3-rules block repeated at prompt END** (lost-in-the-middle; rules currently sit mid-prompt).
14. **Domain knowledge blocks** (e.g. the frontend design rubric from round 1) gated by intent — applies the same "inject expertise the weak model lacks" pattern to any domain.

Empirical agent will confirm which fire most in practice. Holding for it before I start editing — it's the ground truth that should reorder this list.

Want me to **start implementing Tier 0 now** (the tool-use fixes — highest certainty, fixes the root cause), or wait for the empirical results and present the full reordered plan first?

# Empirical Failure Catalogue — glint-cli (groq/compound agent)

Method: 7 controlled headless runs in `/tmp/glint-test-0{1..7}` (default `medium` effort, `--yolo`), each filesystem-verified independently and cross-checked against its hash-chained diagnostics trace in `~/.glint/diagnostics/traces-2026-06-13.jsonl`. Bottom line: the agent is **better than "sucks at everything"** on simple single-shot file/bash/search tasks — 6 of 7 of my tasks produced a correct final filesystem state. The real, reproducible failures are concentrated in: (1) **bad first-round planning / wrong-order parallel tool calls**, (2) **verify-nudge pressure driving destructive edits + uncaught false success claims**, and (3) **hallucinated `await_agents` calls**. These are quality/correctness failures, not total breakdown.

## Log-mining ground truth (free evidence)

Today's traces, nudge tallies: `empty_nudge` ×48, `verify_nudge` ×10, `failure_nudge` ×2, `reality_nudge` ×1. Tool usage skews heavily to `read_file` (85) and `ls` (54).
